239.title: Buddhism: the man under the tree
239.hook: Siddhartha leaves a palace, sits under a tree at Bodh Gaya, and wakes up
239.howItsDone: Buddhists around the world tell the story of the Buddha's leaving home and awakening, and many make pilgrimage to Bodh Gaya, where a descendant of the Bodhi tree still grows beside the Mahabodhi Temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali, the row of lamps that closed our Hindu visit. Your line was light over dark. Day two hundred thirty-nine, and a new visit: Buddhism.

A palace. A beautiful family, servants, music, a future as king, and a father determined that his son will never see anything sad. Then one day the son sees it anyway. Old age. Sickness. A body being carried to be burned. And a wandering holy man, calm in the middle of it all. It can't be unseen. In the story Buddhists tell, that's how a young prince named Siddhartha Gautama walked out of his palace one night and went looking for a way through.
screen: `A PALACE, AND A FATHER'S PLAN.` → `OLD AGE, SICKNESS, DEATH, A MONK.` → `THE PRINCE WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Siddhartha was born in Lumbini, in what's now southern Nepal, into the Shakya clan, in a century scholars still debate. The four sights, the old man, the sick man, the corpse and the monk, come from later biographies, and Buddhists treasure them as the heart of why he left. As a young man he left home, and for years he tried what the holy men of his day taught, including fasting so hard, the texts say, that he could feel his spine through his stomach. It didn't work. So he did something his companions thought was giving up: he ate. A bowl of rice and milk, offered, in the traditional story, by a young woman named Sujata. Then he sat down under a tree at a place now called Bodh Gaya, in northern India, and resolved not to get up until he understood. The tradition says Mara, the tempter, came with fear and desire and doubt, and that Siddhartha touched the earth as his witness. Through the night he saw clearly, and by dawn, Buddhists say, he had woken up. That's the name: the word Buddha is formed from a root meaning to wake. The Buddha is the awakened one, and the tree became the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. Buddhists honor him not as a creator god but as a teacher who found the way and showed it. The texts even say he hesitated to teach at first, thinking no one would understand. Then he got up and walked to find his old companions.

segments.voice: If you're near a tree, sit with your back to it; if not, picture a wide, shady tree above you, its leaves moving. Rest a hand on something solid: the ground, the floor, your knee. Then just be awake to what's here, the sounds, the air, your breathing, with nothing to become.
Buddhism. The path of the Buddha, the awakened one: a prince who left his palace, sat under a tree at Bodh Gaya, and woke up. Today's word.
Your line: wake up. Tomorrow, the first thing he taught. Day two hundred thirty-nine, done.

240.title: Buddhism: the first truth
240.hook: life is marked by unsatisfactoriness, and there is a way through (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
240.howItsDone: Buddhists study the four noble truths as a foundation of the teaching, and Theravada communities chant the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, on festival days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prince under the tree who woke up. Your line was wake up. Day two hundred forty.

You finally get the thing. The phone, the job, the apartment, the relationship status. For about a week it's wonderful. Then something is slightly off. The phone is already old. The job has a boss. The apartment has a neighbor with a drum kit. It isn't a tragedy. Just a faint sense that things never quite land. After the Buddha woke up, he walked to a deer park and gave his first teaching, and the first of the truths he named there was that feeling. Its name is dukkha.
screen: `YOU FINALLY GET THE THING.` → `SOMETHING IS SLIGHTLY OFF.` → `DUKKHA.`

segments.voice: That first teaching was at the Deer Park near Varanasi, to the five companions who had once fasted with him. Buddhists call it the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching, and it's recorded in the Samyutta Nikaya, a collection in the Pali Canon. In it he lays out four noble truths, which later teachers compare to a doctor's diagnosis. First, the illness: dukkha. Second, its cause: craving, a thirst that keeps grasping. Third, the good news: it can end. Fourth, the cure: a path, the noble eightfold path. Dukkha is often translated suffering, and that's part of it: birth, aging, sickness and death, being stuck with what you don't want, being parted from what you love. But the word is wider than pain. It's also stress, friction, unsatisfactoriness: the sense that even pleasant things can't fully satisfy, because they change and pass. Some teachers explain dukkha with a wheel on a badly fitted axle, so every ride is a little bumpy; scholars doubt that's where the word comes from, but the picture fits. So the first truth isn't the Buddha saying life is miserable, full stop. It's the first of four. A doctor who names your illness isn't being gloomy; he's starting treatment. The third truth says it plainly: craving can fade and cease. The whole point of naming dukkha is the fourth truth: there's a way through.

segments.voice: Let something that's bothering you come up, small or not, and feel it without the story: not who did what, or why it's unfair. Where is it in your body: tight, heavy, restless? Name it plainly, this is dukkha, and keep breathing beside it.
Dukkha. Pali for suffering, stress, unsatisfactoriness: the first of the Buddha's four noble truths, named so it can be healed. Today's word.

241.title: Buddhism: everything changes
241.howItsDone: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation, watching sensations, thoughts and breath arise and pass, and many chant verses on impermanence, especially at funerals and memorials.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukkha, the first noble truth. Your line was there's a way through. Day two hundred forty-one.

Scroll back through your photos five years. The haircut. The friends you don't see anymore. The apartment. The face, a bit younger. Nothing dramatic happened, and yet almost everything is different. It's easy to know this and still treat the good things as if they'll stay exactly as they are, and the bad things as if they'll last forever. The Buddha named this as one of the main reasons life never quite satisfies, and, surprisingly, one of the main ways through. Its Pali name: anicca.
screen: `FIVE YEARS OF PHOTOS.` → `THE GOOD WILL STAY, THE BAD WILL LAST.` → `ANICCA.`

segments.voice: Anicca is a Pali word. Nicca means lasting, constant; the a in front means not. So anicca: not lasting, impermanent. Buddhists count it among the three marks of everything that exists, alongside dukkha, and a third, not-self, which is a lesson for another day. The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse, gives it in verse two hundred seventy-seven. In Max Müller's 1881 translation it begins: "All created things perish." Everything that's put together, that arises from causes, will come apart. Mountains, bodies, moods, friendships, empires, this breath. The verse goes on: whoever sees this clearly grows weary of suffering, and that is the path to purity. Here's the turn. Impermanence sounds like bad news, and part of it is: it's why pleasant things never fully satisfy. But look at it the other way. The terrible week will also pass. Anger, even as it flares, is already changing. The habit you hate is not carved in stone. If everything were permanent, nothing could heal and no one could grow. Impermanence is also what makes the way through possible. Buddhist texts record that as the Buddha lay dying, his last words to his followers returned to this: all things that are put together fall apart, so keep going, with care. Not a sad line. A practical one. So the carry is two small words you can say to anything, good or bad: this too. This too will change.
screen: `NICCA: LASTING. ANICCA: NOT.` · `ALL CREATED THINGS PERISH.` · `THE BAD WEEK PASSES TOO.` · `THE LAST WORDS: KEEP GOING.` · then, large: `THIS TOO.`

segments.voice: Watch your breath and notice that no two breaths are the same: one longer, one catching, one soft. Then widen out to sounds coming and going, an itch that arrives and fades, a thought that flares and dissolves. Each time you notice something pass, say inside: this too.
Anicca. Pali for impermanence: everything put together changes and passes, the good and the bad. Today's word.
Your line: this too. Said to something good, it helps you enjoy it fully; said to something hard, it helps you bear it. That's day two hundred forty-one.

242.title: Buddhism: loving-kindness
242.hook: may all beings be happy and at ease (Sutta Nipata 1.8)
242.howItsDone: Many Buddhists chant the Karaniya Metta Sutta and practice metta meditation, offering goodwill in turn to themselves, a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person and all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anicca, everything changes. Your line was this too. Day two hundred forty-two.

Think about the way a mother looks at her newborn asleep. Nothing is being asked of that baby. It hasn't earned anything or done anything useful. And the love is total: she'd step in front of a truck for it. Now imagine even a small slice of that toward the person ahead of you in line. Toward the driver who cut you off. Toward every living creature, seen and unseen. It sounds impossible. The Buddha taught that it can be practiced, a little at a time, like a muscle. Today's word: metta.
screen: `A MOTHER AND A SLEEPING BABY.` → `THE PERSON AHEAD OF YOU IN LINE.` → `METTA.`

segments.voice: Metta is Pali, often translated loving-kindness or goodwill. It's related to the word for a friend, so you could also hear it as friendliness: wishing someone well the way a true friend does. The most famous teaching on it is a short text in the Sutta Nipata, one of the oldest parts of the Pali Canon, called the discourse on loving-kindness. Buddhist tradition tells that it was first given to a group of monks who were frightened while meditating in a forest. It begins with character: be capable, upright, gentle, not proud, content with little. Then it opens out into wishing. May all beings be happy and at ease. And it lists them, so no one is left out: weak or strong, tall or short, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, those already born and those yet to be born. Then comes the picture from the hook. Just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let a person cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Many Buddhists across schools practice metta in meditation, often in a traditional order: first toward yourself, then someone you love, then someone neutral, then someone difficult, and finally all beings everywhere. The phrases are simple and often quiet: may you be well, may you be happy, may you be safe. The idea isn't to fake a feeling. It's to keep pointing the heart in a direction, until the direction becomes a habit.
screen: `METTA: GOODWILL, FRIENDLINESS.` · `SEEN OR UNSEEN, NEAR OR FAR.` · `AS A MOTHER GUARDS HER ONLY CHILD.` · `YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, A FOE.` · then, large: `MAY ALL BEINGS BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Wish three people well, the way many Buddhists do: first someone easy to love, then someone neutral, like a neighbor or a cashier, then, if you're willing, someone a little difficult, not the hardest person. To each, inside, offer the traditional wish: may you be well, may you be happy. Then let it spread wider.
Metta. Pali for loving-kindness, friendliness, goodwill: wishing all beings happiness, as a mother guards her only child. Today's word.
Your line: may all beings be well. It's a wish with no one left out. Day two hundred forty-two, done.

243.title: Buddhism: the middle way
243.hook: neither indulgence nor harshness, the Buddha's first teaching (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
243.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the Buddha's path as the middle way between indulgence and self-mortification, practiced as the noble eightfold path; teachers tell the story of Sona's lute to people who push themselves too hard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, metta, loving-kindness. Your line was may all beings be well. Day two hundred forty-three.

January. The plan is to change everything: up at five, cold showers, no sugar, no screens, a run every day. By the third week the plan is in pieces, and by February there's cereal straight from the box at midnight. Then the cycle starts again: too much, then too little. The Buddha knew that swing from the inside. He'd lived both ends of it, the palace and the starving years. So the first thing he taught about the path was where to walk. Today: Buddhism's middle way.
screen: `UP AT FIVE, COLD SHOWERS.` → `CEREAL AT MIDNIGHT.` → `THE SWING, AND THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Back to the Deer Park, and the five companions who had watched Siddhartha starve himself, then walked away from him when he ate. When the Buddha came back to them, the Samyutta Nikaya records, the very first thing he said, even before the four noble truths, was about two extremes to avoid. One is chasing sense pleasures: low, he says, and not leading anywhere good. The other is tormenting yourself: painful, and just as useless. He'd tried both. Between them, he said, there's a middle way, which leads to clear seeing, to peace and to awakening. And he names it: the noble eightfold path. Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The middle isn't lukewarm. It's balance that works. Another collection, the Anguttara Nikaya, has a lovely story about this. A monk named Sona practiced so hard, walking in meditation, that his feet bled, and still he got nowhere. He was ready to quit and go home. The Buddha came to him and asked: before you became a monk, you played the lute, didn't you? When the strings were too tight, did it sound good? No. Too loose? No. And when they were tuned, not too tight, not too loose? Then it sounded just right. Effort is like that, the Buddha told him. Too much makes you restless, too little makes you lazy. Tune it. Sona did, and the texts say he went on to awakening.
screen: `TWO EXTREMES: INDULGE OR TORMENT.` · `BETWEEN THEM, A PATH.` · `THE NOBLE EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `SONA'S LUTE: TUNE THE STRINGS.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Tune your sitting first: if you're straining, too upright, jaw tight, loosen a little; if you're slumping or drifting, lift a little, until you find the tuned string. Then pick one habit you swing on, food, exercise, work, your phone, and picture the too-tight version and the too-loose one. Now picture the middle: something you could actually keep.
Buddhism's middle way. Neither indulgence nor self-torment: the path between them, named in the Buddha's first teaching. Today's word.
Your line: the middle. Not the heroic version, not the collapse, but the one you could keep every day. See you tomorrow.

244.title: Buddhism: three refuges
244.hook: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the teaching and the community
244.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the three refuges, usually three times over, at the start of practice and at ceremonies; taking refuge formally is a common way of becoming Buddhist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona's lute and the middle way. Your line was the middle. Day two hundred forty-four.

Where do you go when it rains hard? Not weather rain. The phone call with bad news, the month that goes sideways. Shelters like that often go unnamed: a person to call first, a place, a book or a song. Buddhists name theirs, very precisely. Three shelters, said aloud, often three times over, at the start of practice, at ceremonies, at the moment someone becomes a Buddhist. The third one is today's word: sangha.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU GO WHEN IT RAINS?` → `THREE NAMED SHELTERS.` → `SANGHA.`

segments.voice: The three refuges, sometimes called the three jewels, are a short formula at the heart of Buddhist life. In Pali they begin: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." I go to the Buddha for refuge. Then the dhamma, the teaching. Then the sangha, the community. Then the whole thing is said a second time, and a third. Saraṇa, refuge, means a shelter, a safe place, somewhere to stand. Buddhists explain it this way. The Buddha is the example: proof, they say, that a human being can wake up. The dhamma is the map: the teaching and the path from this week, the four truths, impermanence, loving-kindness, the middle way. And the sangha is the company for the road. Sangha means a gathering, a community, and Buddhists use it in more than one way. In its traditional sense, it means the community of monks and nuns, who keep the teaching alive and are supported by lay Buddhists with food and care. In another sense, it means the noble community: all those who've truly begun to wake up, in any age. And some Buddhists today, especially in the West, use sangha for the whole community of practitioners, lay and monastic. There's an exchange in the Samyutta Nikaya: the Buddha's attendant Ananda says good friendship is half of the holy life, and the Buddha corrects him. Not half, Ananda. The whole of it. A path this long isn't meant to be walked alone.
screen: `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `SARANA: A SHELTER.` · `EXAMPLE, MAP, COMPANY.` · `NOT HALF: THE WHOLE OF IT.` · then, large: `THREE REFUGES.`

segments.voice: Borrow the Buddhist shape, without the vow, and ask yourself three quiet questions: who shows me that a better way is possible, what words do I come back to when it's hard, and who walks with me? Let a face, a line, a group come for each, and just notice them. Be grateful if gratitude comes.
Sangha. Pali for community: the third of Buddhism's three refuges, after the Buddha and the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: three refuges. An example, a map, and company for the road. That's day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Vesak, the full moon
245.hook: many Buddhists mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on the full moon of Vesakha
245.howItsDone: On Vesak many Buddhists visit temples, offer flowers and lamps, keep extra precepts, listen to teachings and give food and help; in Sri Lanka streets fill with lanterns and free food stalls called dansal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha, the teaching and the sangha. Your line was three refuges. Day two hundred forty-five, the last day of this Buddhist visit.

Night in Colombo, in Sri Lanka. Streets hung with paper lanterns, some towering over the people below, lit from inside. Free food stalls handing out rice and tea to anyone passing, no money asked. White-clad families walking to the temple with flowers and oil lamps. And overhead, a full moon. Across Asia and far beyond, many Buddhists keep this night as a high point of their year. The Buddhist visit closes with it. Vesak, the full moon.
screen: `LANTERNS OVER EVERY STREET.` → `FREE FOOD, NO MONEY ASKED.` → `VESAK, THE FULL MOON.`

segments.voice: Vesak takes its name from Vesakha, a month in the old Indian calendar, and the festival falls on its full moon, usually in April or May. In the Theravada tradition, followed in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, Buddhists hold that three great events in the Buddha's life all happened on that same full moon: his birth in Lumbini, his awakening under the tree at Bodh Gaya, and his passing into final nirvana at Kushinagar. One night for a whole life. Other Buddhist traditions keep the calendar differently. In much of East Asia, the Buddha's birthday is its own festival, and in Japan his awakening is often marked separately, in December. In Tibet, a whole holy month, Saga Dawa, marks these events. So once again, who you ask matters. For such a big night, what people do on Vesak is quiet. They visit the temple, offer flowers, light lamps and incense. Many keep extra precepts for the day, eating simply and avoiding harm. And they give: food, lanterns, help. On the Buddha's birthday in East Asia, people pour scented water over a small statue of the baby Buddha. In 1999 the United Nations recognized the Day of Vesak internationally. And that closes the week with Buddhists. The man under the tree who woke up. Dukkha, and the way through. Anicca, this too. Metta, may all beings be well. The middle way and Sona's lute. The three refuges. And a full moon to hold them all.
screen: `VESAKHA: THE MONTH'S FULL MOON.` · `BIRTH, AWAKENING, PASSING.` · `EACH TRADITION'S OWN CALENDAR.` · `FLOWERS, LAMPS, GIVING.` · then, large: `THE FULL MOON.`

segments.voice: If the moon is up and you can see it, go and look; if not, picture a full moon rising over a temple roof, round and white. Let one thing from this week come back to you, and let the moon hold it.
